answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in her own words: the line comes from the “Autobiographical Notes” Marie Curie wrote for Pierre Curie (The Macmillan Company, 1923), recalling her first self-taught experiments in a small Warsaw laboratory. Her original reads “the way of progress is neither swift nor easy.”

source.excerpt: At times I would be encouraged by a little unhoped-for success, at others I would be in the deepest despair because of accidents and failures resulting from my inexperience. But on the whole, though I was taught that the way of progress is neither swift nor easy, this first trial confirmed in me the taste for experimental research in the fields of physics and chemistry.
trail: The sentence appears verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of Pierre Curie ↗: “though I was taught that the way of progress is neither swift nor easy.”
It sits within Curie’s own Autobiographical Notes, first published by The Macmillan Company in 1923 ↗, where she describes her first experiments in a Warsaw laboratory.
Quote aggregators reproduce the line with no real source — Wikiquote ↗ even cites a 2002 software-engineering manual, showing how the sentence circulates unmoored from its origin.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version lifts out the middle clause and changes ‘is’ to ‘was’
source.excerptNote: In the original this is not a free-standing maxim — it is a subordinate clause inside Curie’s account of teaching herself experimental science, working only evenings and Sundays in a small municipal laboratory in Warsaw directed by one of her cousins.
source.rightsNote: Pierre Curie was published in 1923 and is in the public domain in the United States; it is freely readable via Project Gutenberg ↗ and the Internet Archive ↗.

author.heading: About Marie Curie
author.metaLine: 1867–1934 · physicist and chemist, two-time Nobel laureate
author.bio: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Marie Curie was a Polish-French physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity — a term she and Pierre coined. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences: Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911). She wrote her brief autobiographical notes in 1923 at the urging of the American journalist Marie Mattingly Meloney, appending them to her memoir of her late husband Pierre.

misattribution.heading: What travels with the quote
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Marie Curie is correct — but the wording and the sourcing that usually accompany it are not.

items.why: The famous form uses the past tense (“was neither swift nor easy”) as a stand-alone maxim; Curie’s original in Pierre Curie (1923) ↗ uses the present tense (“is”) inside a longer sentence about her first experiments.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with a citation to Java Connector Architecture (2002), a software-engineering manual — not to Curie’s 1923 book, where it actually originates.

misattribution.truthLine: The quote is genuinely Marie Curie’s, from the Autobiographical Notes in Pierre Curie (1923) ↗ — where she wrote that “the way of progress is neither swift nor easy.”

context.heading: Where it comes from
lead: Marie Curie was famously reluctant to talk about herself. She wrote her brief Autobiographical Notes in 1923 only at the insistence of the American journalist Marie Mattingly Meloney, to accompany a memoir of her husband Pierre. The line about progress comes from that short memoir — recalling not her Nobel-winning discoveries but her earliest, fumbling experiments as a young woman.

In the passage she is describing teaching herself physics and chemistry in a small municipal laboratory in Warsaw, run by one of her cousins, with time to work only in the evenings and on Sundays — “encouraged by a little unhoped-for success” one day and “in the deepest despair” the next. The famous maxim is really her wry summary of that apprenticeship.
detailsBody: The subtle drift from “is” to “was” changes the tone slightly: the present tense frames it as a standing lesson she carried forward, not a closed chapter. Quote sites almost universally print the past-tense version, stripped of the surrounding sentence about her first trial at experimental research.
